title: What If Kids' Behavior Is the Symptom, Not the Problem
author: Stinehart, Kevin
summary: Kevin Stinehart uses the Lincoln Memorial's deterioration story as the framing metaphor for a systemic critique of how schools respond to challenging student behavior. Just as the Memorial's damage came from cleaning chemicals deployed against bird droppings caused by lights that attracted insects -- with the fix being to turn the lights on later, not scrub harder -- Stinehart argues that schools are responding to behavioral symptoms (meltdowns, dysregulation, social failure) with ever-more-sophisticated management systems rather than addressing the root cause: children are less practiced at the basic developmental work of being human. The root cause is the systematic removal of the conditions in which developmental capacities naturally grow: unstructured play, neighborhood life, mixed-age interaction, boredom, small risks, and child-led problem-solving. His Architecture of Childhood framework (covering nine developmental domains from self-regulation to physical health to executive function) presents these not as nine decorative categories but as load-bearing structures that appear only when materials -- the right conditions and experiences -- are present. The article reports on his school's experience opening unstructured playground time through Let Grow's Play Club model, finding that children naturally exercised executive function, social negotiation, and resilience without any adult instruction. Stinehart concludes with a challenge to improvement science: when the same behavioral problems keep appearing across classrooms, grades, and communities, the question is not which intervention works but what conditions upstream are missing.
points: * Children's widespread behavioral difficulties are symptoms of a depleted developmental habitat, not evidence that children are inherently worse -- the kids these days explanation is emotionally satisfying but diagnostically wrong. * Capacities like self-regulation, social connection, resilience, and executive function cannot be directly instructed into children; they emerge from conditions -- real discomfort, real conflict, real risk, real boredom -- that modern schools and childhoods systematically remove. * The category error hiding in SEL curricula and behavior systems is the assumption that the missing capacity can be taught through lessons; in reality, a well-managed child is not the same thing as a developed child. * Unstructured play is the most powerful developmental environment available because it exercises social, emotional, physical, cognitive, moral, and imaginative capacities simultaneously -- schools like clean categories; play refuses to stay in one. * The diagnostic question Stinehart proposes: when the same problems keep reappearing across grades and cohorts, stop asking which intervention and start asking what conditions are producing this mess, and what would have to change upstream.
quotes: I think school systems have gotten really efficient at scrubbing the marble.
A lot of children are just less practiced at the basic work of being human. That changes the whole conversation.
There is a category mistake hiding in plain sight. Many of the capacities schools keep trying to teach cannot be taught. They have to be grown.

Children do not develop self-regulation in the abstract. They develop it in the middle of life, when they are disappointed, excited, tired, left out, corrected, challenged, overstimulated, told no, bored, embarrassed, and then slowly learn that none of those has to become the end of the world.

A good stretch of unstructured play is doing far more than adults can see from a distance. Children are reading faces, tracking rules, testing strength, managing impulses, inventing worlds, negotiating power, recovering from embarrassment, handling exclusion, taking small risks, learning to communicate, and deciding whether the fun is worth the discomfort. It is physical, social, emotional, imaginative, moral, and cognitive all at once.

We want the finished capacities without restoring the experiences that build them. We want calm bodies with fewer chances to move. We want collaborative children with less chances to collaborate in low-stakes settings.
A well-managed child is not the same thing as a developed child. That distinction may be one of the most important lines school systems need to recover.

If the same problems keep appearing across classrooms, grade levels, families, and communities, the problem is probably bigger than the individual motivation that we keep focusing on. We have to look at the broader conditions around the child.
